How Much House Can You Afford? A Practical Guide to Home Affordability

Quick Tool Access: Need to compute your numbers right now? Jump straight to our free Interactive Calculator with real-time in-browser calculations.

Direct Answer: You can afford a home where total monthly housing costs stay under 28% of gross monthly income, and total debts remain under 36%. On a $100,000 household salary with zero debts, your maximum affordable monthly payment is $2,333, supporting a $350,000 to $400,000 home purchase.

The 28/36 Rule: How Mortgage Lenders Evaluate Affordability

When underwriting conventional residential mortgages, underwriting guidelines established by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac emphasize the Debt-to-Income (DTI) ratio. Financial planners and mortgage underwriters evaluate two critical percentages:

Front-End DTI = (Total Monthly Housing Costs / Gross Monthly Income) × 100 ≤ 28%
Back-End DTI = (Total Housing Costs + Recurring Monthly Debts / Gross Monthly Income) × 100 ≤ 36%

Understanding Front-End Housing Costs (PITI + HOA):

  • P: Principal repayment.
  • I: Mortgage interest.
  • T: Municipal real estate property taxes.
  • I: Homeowners hazard insurance premium (and PMI if applicable).
  • HOA: Mandatory homeowners association or condo maintenance fees.

While some government-backed programs (such as FHA loans) allow back-end DTI limits up to 43% (or even 50% with automated underwriting compensating factors), stretching beyond 36% severely restricts household discretionary cash flow, creating the classic "house-poor" predicament.

Salary to House Affordability Benchmarks

The table below provides a realistic reference model based on the standard 28% front-end guideline, assuming a 30-year fixed loan at 6.5% interest, 1.2% annual property tax rate, $1,200 annual insurance, and zero HOA dues:

Annual Gross Salary Monthly Gross Income Max Monthly Housing (28%) Affordable Price (10% Down) Affordable Price (20% Down)
$50,000 $4,167 $1,167 $155,000 $185,000
$75,000 $6,250 $1,750 $245,000 $290,000
$100,000 $8,333 $2,333 $335,000 $395,000
$125,000 $10,417 $2,917 $425,000 $500,000
$150,000 $12,500 $3,500 $515,000 $605,000
$200,000 $16,667 $4,667 $695,000 $815,000

Worked Example: Real Calculation with Non-Mortgage Debt

Let us analyze a real-world scenario you can test right now in our Home Affordability Calculator:

  • Annual Household Gross Salary: $110,000 ($9,166.67 per month)
  • Existing Monthly Debt Payments: $450 (car note) + $250 (student loan) = $700.00/month
  • Available Cash for Down Payment: $60,000.00
  • Estimated Interest Rate: 6.50% (30-year fixed)

Calculation Steps:

  1. Front-End Test (28% of $9,166.67): $2,566.67 max housing expense.
  2. Back-End Test (36% of $9,166.67): $3,300.00 total debt limit. Subtracting $700 existing debts leaves $2,600.00 available for housing.
  3. Underwriter chooses the lower of the two limits: $2,566.67 per month.
  4. Subtracting estimated property taxes ($380/mo) and insurance ($110/mo) leaves $2,076.67 for Principal & Interest.
  5. At 6.5% for 360 months, $2,076.67 supports a mortgage loan amount of $328,500.00.
  6. Adding the $60,000 down payment yields a Maximum Affordable Purchase Price of $388,500.00.

The Critical Role of Down Payment: 5% vs. 10% vs. 20%

While 20% down payment is the gold standard for avoiding Private Mortgage Insurance (PMI), many buyers purchase with 3% to 10% down. Here is how that choice alters your economics on a $400,000 purchase at 6.5%:

Down Payment Tier Cash Required Loan Amount Monthly P&I Est. Monthly PMI Total Monthly Payment
5% Down $20,000.00 $380,000.00 $2,401.86 $220.00 $2,621.86
10% Down $40,000.00 $360,000.00 $2,275.45 $150.00 $2,425.45
20% Down $80,000.00 $320,000.00 $2,022.61 $0.00 $2,022.61

Reaching 20% down saves $599.25 per month ($7,191 annually) in recurring housing costs compared to a 5% down payment.

Hidden Costs That Shrink Homebuying Budgets

  1. Closing Costs (2% to 5%): On a $400,000 home, lender origination fees, title search, escrow reserves, and transfer stamps cost between $8,000 and $20,000 in cash.
  2. The 1% Annual Maintenance Rule: Single-family homes require roughly 1% to 2% of the home value each year ($4,000 to $8,000 annually) for HVAC maintenance, roof repairs, plumbing, and wear.
  3. Emergency Reserve Buffer: Do not drain your savings account to zero for the down payment. Lenders generally require 2 months of PITI reserves, and prudent financial planning dictates keeping a 3-to-6-month living fund.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the standard rule of thumb for house affordability by salary?

Lenders commonly follow the 28/36 debt-to-income (DTI) guideline. Your total monthly housing payment (PITI + HOA) should not exceed 28% of gross monthly income (front-end ratio), and total recurring debt payments (housing + student loans, car loans, credit cards) should not exceed 36% (back-end ratio).

How much house can I afford with an $80,000 salary?

With an $80,000 annual gross salary ($6,667/month), 28% allows a maximum monthly housing cost of $1,867. Assuming a 6.5% interest rate, 20% down payment, and standard property taxes/insurance, this typically supports a purchase price between $280,000 and $325,000 depending on existing debts.

Why does existing non-mortgage debt reduce borrowing capacity so heavily?

Lenders enforce the back-end DTI cap. If you earn $7,000 gross per month, your absolute debt ceiling at 36% is $2,520. If you have a $500 car note and $300 student loan, your available housing payment shrinks from $2,520 down to $1,720, cutting your purchasing power by over $120,000.

How does down payment size change monthly mortgage payments?

A larger down payment lowers the principal borrowed and eliminates Private Mortgage Insurance (PMI) if reaching 20%. On a $400,000 home at 6.5%, putting 20% down ($80,000) results in a monthly P&I of $2,022.61, whereas putting 5% down ($20,000) increases P&I to $2,401.86 plus roughly $190/month in PMI.

What additional costs besides down payment must homebuyers budget for?

Buyers need 2% to 5% of the loan amount for closing costs (title insurance, loan origination, appraisal, transfer taxes) plus 3 to 6 months of living expenses in an emergency cash reserve following closing.
